paper_title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/

sections.content: Human demonstrations provide rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Introduction People routinely manipulate objects with both hands, such as holding bottle while opening its lid. Learning such dexterous skills from human demonstrations offers natural approach to robotic manipulation [5, 36, 37, 46]. However, differences between human and robot hands prevent demonstrations from being directly replayed on robots. Recent methods bridge this gap by retargeting human motions to robot hands and training policies in simulation to track 1 demonstrated object trajectories [21, 30, 63]. Nevertheless, fundamental limitation of these methods is their reliance on object trajectory tracking as the primary learning objective. Even when robot accurately tracks the demonstrated trajectory, its hands may contact the wrong object parts or slide on the object, resulting in unstable manipulation. Faithful bimanual manipulation requires not only reproducing where the object moves, but also preserving how the hands interact with it. However, achieving contact-preserving bimanual manipulation presents three key challenges. First, bimanual manipulation requires coordinated yet role-specific control. Existing methods either control both hands through unified policy [30, 63] or train separate policies independently [62], limiting explicit coordination or shared learning between hands. Second, preserving human hand-object contacts across different embodiments remains difficult. Although existing methods incorporate contact-related rewards [22, 30, 63], robot hands can still contact the object differently from human hands, particularly in which hand holds an object part and whether the contact is maintained. Third, learning complex demonstrations is hindered by difficult manipulation phases. To make training tractable, prior methods assist the object early in training, with virtual object controller (VOC), proportional-derivative (PD) controller that pulls the object toward its demonstrated trajectory [30, 63], or with relaxed physics [21], and gradually withdraw this assistance. However, the assistance is typically reduced uniformly across the demonstration, allowing difficult phase, such as handover, to stall the entire training process. To address these challenges, we introduce DexDuet, framework for learning contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from single human demonstration  (Fig. 1)  . To coordinate the two hands, DexDuet factorizes the bimanual policy into two per-hand policies that share network parameters while observing each others states. This allows each hand to perform its own role, adapt to its partner, and benefit from shared learning. To preserve human hand-object interactions, DexDuet introduces two complementary interaction rewards. The first encourages each robot hand to match the orientation and finger configuration of its human counterpart relative to the object. The second encourages each hand region, such as the palm or finger, to contact the object where the corresponding human region does. Together, these rewards guide the robot to reproduce the demonstrated contacts rather than merely track object motion. Furthermore, to facilitate learning through difficult manipulation phases, we propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts VOC assistance separately for each demonstration segment based on its learning progress. It also initializes episodes from previously reached states and prioritizes failing segments, enabling the policy to learn complex demonstrations without assistance. In summary, our contributions are: We present DexDuet, framework for learning contactpreserving bimanual dexterity from human demonstrations through factorized, weight-sharing per-hand policies that enable role-specific control and partner-aware coordination. We introduce two complementary interaction rewards that preserve human hand-object interactions by aligning object-relative hand configurations and region-level contacts across different robot embodiments. We propose assisted reference-state initialization (ARSI), an adaptive curriculum that combines segmentspecific VOC assistance, initialization from previously reached states, and failure-aware sampling to improve learning through difficult manipulation phases. We evaluate DexDuet on four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, demonstrating consistent improvements in object tracking and contact preservation, with additional demonstrations on two real robot systems. 2. Related Work Learning dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations. Human demonstrations are natural source of dexterous skills, because people handle everyday objects with both hands skillfully. Many works therefore collect demonstrations of hand-object interaction. They capture them in motion-capture and multi-camera studios [2, 6, 43] or with wearable gloves, exoskeletons and headsets [1, 44, 46, 51], reconstruct them from monocular or egocentric videos [7, 33, 36, 59], or generate them with models trained on such data [58]. These efforts have produced large datasets of hand-object interaction [9, 16, 26, 60]. However, these demonstrations cannot be replayed directly on robot, because robot hands differ from human hands in size, kinematics and actuation. For humanoid robots and physics-based characters, common solution to this gap maps the human motion onto the target body and trains policy in physics simulation to track it [14, 23, 47, 52]. Recent methods apply the same idea to dexterous hands. They train policies that move the object along its demonstrated trajectory, guided by the retargeted hand motion [5, 8, 21, 22, 25, 27, 30, 38, 53, 63], or optimize the control sequence directly [24, 34]. These methods are primarily driven by an object-tracking reward. Some of them also compare the robots contacts with the humans frame by frame, either by their locations [19, 22, 30] or by the forces and torques they can exert on the object [63]. These terms act on individual contacts in each frame, and none of them considers whether contact stays fixed on the object over time. The robot can therefore still move the object along its trajectory with different contacts, for example with the other hand or 2 with sliding fingers, which makes the manipulation unstable. DexDuet instead trains each robot hand to preserve the humans contacts, so that it stays on the part that the humans hand holds without sliding. Bimanual manipulation. Two hands that manipulate one object must coordinate, because each performs its own part of the task and the task fails as soon as either one fails. Imitation-learning policies for two robot arms build this coordination into their architecture, for example with per-arm modules that exchange information or predict shared future state [3, 12, 17, 20, 31, 49, 50, 56]. In reinforcement learning of bimanual dexterous tasks, coordination has been eased by treating each hand as separate agent [4], by giving the two hands complementary roles [54], or by training one hand before both [61]. Methods that transfer human demonstrations to two dexterous hands have not used these ideas. They either drive both hands with one policy, possibly on top of per-hand imitators [21, 30, 63], or learn an independent policy for each hand [62]. With single policy, the learning of one hand is tied to that of the other, whereas independent policies do not share what one hand learns with the other. DexDuet lies between these two designs, inspired by cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning [55] and by decentralized agents that reason about their partner [13]. Each hand has its own policy, which observes the other hand, and the two policies share one network, so that both coordination and experience sharing are built into the policy. Curricula for dexterous manipulation. Learning dexterous manipulation from complex demonstrations is hard, because policy that starts at the first frame rarely reaches the later phases. Tracking methods therefore also start episodes at later frames of the demonstration, either from reference states [63] or from states the policy has already reached [22, 52, 53], and some sample the start frames more often where the policy fails [23]. second technique assists the object, with VOC [30, 63] or with relaxed physics [21, 24], and reduces this assistance over training. However, the assistance is reduced uniformly across the entire demonstration, even though the difficulty usually lies in only few phases, so that progress on the whole demonstration is limited by its hardest phase. A-RSI instead sets the assistance separately for each segment of the demonstration, lowering it when the episodes that start there succeed and raising it when they fail, and starts episodes preferentially in segments with high failure rates. hard phase thus keeps its assistance and receives more practice, and training on the rest of the demonstration proceeds independently of it. 3. In dexterous retargeting, reference state consists of the hand configurations of the reference motion and the demonstrated object state of frame. RSI then faces two problems. First, reference state is usually not physically valid, because the retargeted fingers often leave gap to the object or penetrate it. Without valid grasp, an object that starts in the air falls or is pushed away before the policy can act. Second, uniform sampling spends most episodes on phases that the policy has already solved instead of on the difficult one. Assisted referencestate initialization (A-RSI, Fig. 2c and Fig. S2) addresses the first problem by assisting the object, which makes reference states usable, and by starting episodes from states that the policy has reached. Experiments Our experiments address four questions: Q1 Does DexDuet track the object better than the compared baselines for different benchmarks? Q2 Does it preserve the humans hand-object contacts? Q3 Can the learned motions be executed on real robot hands? Q4 What do the per-hand policy, A-RSI and the interaction rewards contribute, and at what training cost? 4.1. Experimental Setup Benchmarks and baselines. We evaluate on three dexterous manipulation benchmarks and on humanoid manipulation challenge, each in the simulator of its baseline. The DexMachina [30] and SPIDER [34] suites each have their own seven ARCTIC [6] demonstrations in Genesis [10]. We evaluate DexMachinas released checkpoints for all four hands and rerun SPIDERs official code, which optimizes an open-loop control sequence instead of policy. The ManipTrans suite [21] has ten OakInk2 [60] demonstrations in Isaac Gym [29], and we retrain ManipTrans with its official protocol. The V2D challenge [32] has 30 humanoid episodes in MuJoCo Warp [11, 45], and we retrain its baseline CHORD [63] with the challenges official PPO and FlashSAC [18] recipes at the same budget of environment steps as DexDuet (Sec. In these pairs, the baselines hand often leaves the part that the humans hand holds, or its fingers slide on it (Fig. 3, first four columns, and Fig. S4). In perceptual study on 24 pairs of runs that track equally well and differ by at least 10 points of Contact-AUC, eleven raters judged the run with the higher Contact-AUC to handle the object more like the human in 251 of 264 judgments (Sec. C.5). DexDuet also holds the object more often after the demonstration ends, with every hand (Tab. 2). The baseline ends the demonstration more than 3 cm from the final pose in 62 of its 140 runs, against 11 for DexDuet (Sec. D.3). 4.3. Real-World Demonstrations Q3: Real robot hands. We replay DexDuets simulated rollouts open-loop on two real setups  (Fig. 4)  . On two Franka arms with Allegro hands, both hands hold bottle above the table and reorient it, following demonstration from OakInk2 [60], and place gamepad, held by both hands, on block. On Unitree G1 humanoid with Inspire hands, the robot lowers box to the floor, puts down bag and pushes an office chair while walking, following human demonstrations reconstructed from video with Do as Do [33]. Its locomotion is handled by whole-body controller in the style of SONIC [28], deployed with RoboQ4: Contribution of each component. Each component prevents different failure (Tab. 3 and Sec. D.4). Without the per-hand policy (e), tracking is less precise in 20 of the 21 runs paired by demonstration and seed. Replacing A-RSI with single-level VOC curriculum (g) lowers Contact-AUC by 6.3 points and requires 20% more updates until training stops (Fig. S3 and Tab. S20). Removing either interaction reward (b, c) lowers Contact-AUC much more than ADD-AUC, and most of this loss lies on windows in which the object stays on track, so it comes from the contacts (Tab. S7). Without both rewards (d), six of the 21 runs fail. 5. Conclusion Prior methods that learn bimanual dexterity from human demonstrations mainly reward object tracking, and their policies often track the object without preserving the humans hand-object contacts. We presented DexDuet, which preserves these contacts with two interaction rewards that compare each robot hand with the human hand relative to the object. To track complex demonstrations, DexDuet also coordinates the two hands with per-hand policies and learns the hard phases with its A-RSI curriculum. Across four benchmarks and five robot embodiments, DexDuet tracks the object and preserves the humans contacts better than prior methods, and its motions are executed on two real 8 robot systems.

S6, in ManipTranss simulator Isaac Gym [29] and its bimanual scene with time step of 1/60 and 2 substeps. This scene models each articulated object as two free rigid bodies. We connect the two by revolute joint at the calibrated pivot and axis, without damping or friction and with limits 5 beyond the range of the demonstration, and train both ManipTrans and DexDuet in this scene with 4,096 parallel environments. The hands are ManipTranss Inspire models with free root bodies, gravity off and linear and angular damping of 20. Their finger joints are positiondriven with stiffness of 500 and damping of 30. PhysX uses the TGS solver with 8 position and 1 velocity iterations, contact offset of 5 mm and rest offset of 0. The friction coefficient is 4.0 on the hands, 2.0 on the object parts and 0.1 on the table. The mass of each part is capped at 0.5 kg. ManipTrans moves each wrist by applying force of at most 8.33 and torque of at most 0.333 per axis to the hands root. DexDuet keeps its own PD law on its six virtual wrist joints, applies the result as force and torque on the root, and caps them at the same values. Isaac Gyms GPU pipeline reports only the net contact force on each body. DexDuet therefore attributes the force on hand link to the object part whose surface lies within 1.5 cm of the link, and uses this attribution in its contact observations 18 and rewards in place of Genesiss per-pair contacts. ManipTrans keeps the schedule on gravity and object friction that it uses during training. V2D challenge. The challenge [32] uses 30 episodes from the challenge dataset and its official evaluator. The episodes are simulated in MuJoCo Warp [11, 45] at 200 Hz with control at 50 Hz. Section B.2 describes how DexDuet is adapted to this humanoid. B.2. DexDuet on the V2D Challenge On the V2D challenge [32], Unitree G1 humanoid reproduces person moving an object, so its Dex3 hands are carried by arms and by body that has to stay balanced. DexDuet keeps its three components on this robot and adapts each of them to the whole body. The observations stay those of the challenges recipe, because the evaluator requires their layout, and we also keep its termination and PPO settings. Policy. The challenges recipe acts through pre-trained whole-body motion tracker [28], which turns the reference motion into targets for the 29 joints of the legs, waist and arms. The policy adds correction to each of these targets and to the reference targets of the 14 finger joints. Because the arms position the hands, each per-hand policy controls one arm and its hand, which makes 14 joints, and third policy controls the 15 joints of the legs and waist. The two per-hand policies share their parameters. Unlike the floating wrists on the tabletop, the arms of the G1 are mirror-image joint chains on common torso, and the challenges observations are expressed in the pelvis frame. We therefore reflect the right arm and hand across the sagittal plane of the pelvis: positions, orientations and joint angles of its inputs and outputs are mapped with the joint signs derived from the URDF, so that the shared policy sees both sides in the convention of the left. As the two hands do in Sec. 3.2, each of the three policies observes the state and the latest joint targets of the other two. As in Sec. 3.2, each has its own probability ratio and value head, and all three receive the same reward. The evaluator accepts single fully connected network, so after training we convert the three policies into one network of that format and verify that it produces the same actions. Curriculum. A-RSI replaces the challenges curriculum and scales the challenges virtual object controller per segment, with segments of 25 frames. An iteration of the challenges PPO recipe collects 98,304 samples, against 384,000 for an update on the DexMachina suite, so we multiply A-RSIs update counts by 3.9 to give each segment the same number of samples between decisions. Keyframes store the full simulator state of the humanoid and the object, and keyframe requires mean tracking reward of at least 0.6, against 0.5 on the DexMachina suite. Episodes that start from reference state in the middle of the demonstration keep the recipes 50-step settling phase, at the end of which the assistance decays to the level of the segment, while keyframe and first-frame starts begin at once. Training is capped at 20,000 iterations, the budget of the retrained CHORD. DexDuet stops earlier on 10 of the 30 episodes, fixed number of iterations after its curriculum has withdrawn all assistance. Rewards. We add two interaction rewards, whose weights keep their ratio to the object-tracking reward from the DexMachina suite. The human targets come from the SOMA [40] hands of the demonstration and are computed once per episode, and the hand-object contact reward treats each object as one part. Both interaction rewards use the three fingers of the Dex3 hand as in Sec. A.4 and Fig. S1, and the fingertip gaps of the human are scaled by 1.5, the retargeting scale of this hand. B.3. Baselines DexMachina is evaluated with the authors released checkpoints. SPIDER is rerun from its official code in our Genesis scene with five seeds per demonstration. SPIDER optimizes each demonstration separately. One run over the 200 frames of demonstration takes 1.419.9 min (median 7.9 min) on one GPU, and the 35 runs take 5.8 in total. ManipTrans is retrained from scratch with its official protocol in the scene with joints. This protocol trains residual policy per demonstration on top of the released perhand imitators, with 4,096 environments, at most 10,000 iterations and early stopping after 1,000 iterations without improvement. To check our ManipTrans setup, we reproduce its evaluation on the 77 OakInk2 validation sequences with the Inspire hand, following the evaluation that the authors describe in their code repository. We obtain success rates of 57.8% on the 38 single-hand sequences and 32.9% on the 39 bimanual ones, against 58.1% and 39.5% in the paper [21]. On successful rollouts, our errors are within 0.06 cm and 0.3 of the reported ones. On the V2D challenge, we retrain CHORD with the challenges official code and both of its recipes for G1 + Dex3. The PPO recipe keeps its settings and runs for 20,000 iterations of 4,096 environments and 24 steps, or 1.97 billion environment steps per episode. On episode 7, the simulator occasionally returns non-finite state that would end learning, so for this episode we reset the affected environment, as our implementation does. The FlashSAC recipe is set for 0.35 billion environment steps, so we scale its settings that depend on the budget, namely the total number of steps, the 19 stage boundaries of its curriculum and the checkpoint interval, to the same 1.97 billion steps and keep everything else. The challenges leaderboard also lists an entry of CHORD, whose training budget is not published and whose policy is not released (Tab. S16). ConTrack [22] is rerun from its official code on the DexMachina suite with XHand hands. We port its environment to the scenes of DexMachinas released XHand runs, with the object not actuated, and keep its rewards, constraint handling, PPO settings and network. It is trained with five seeds per demonstration and DexDuets budget, namely 12,000 environments, 32 steps per update and the same maximum number of updates per demonstration, without early stopping, and, as in ConTrack, we evaluate its final checkpoint. B.4. Training and Evaluation Seeds and stopping. On the DexMachina suite, DexDuet is trained with five seeds per demonstration (15, 24, 42, 66 and 113), and the ablations of Tab. 3 with three (15, 42 and 113). On the SPIDER suite, the five seeds are 15, 24, 42, 43 and 66. On the ManipTrans suite, DexDuet and ManipTrans are both trained with three seeds (42, 24 and 66). On V2D, every method is trained with one seed. On the SPIDER suite, training uses 12,000 parallel environments. On the SPIDER and ManipTrans suites, training takes at most 15,000 updates, the assistance ceiling reaches zero at update 10,000 (a deadline of 9,000 updates plus 1,000update ramp), and training stops 1,500 updates after all assistance is gone. All DexDuet runs that we train in Genesis, including the ablations, use this stopping rule. Evaluation. Every method is evaluated from the first frame of each demonstration, without assistance and with deterministic actions. In Genesis, each policy is evaluated on 100 parallel rollouts, with the first observation read from the simulator after the reset. On the ManipTrans suite, every policy is evaluated on 256 rollouts per demonstration, which are the last two episodes of 128 environments. Every rollout of both methods starts at the first frame of the 200-frame window, whereas ManipTranss own evaluation starts up to 165 frames earlier on seven demonstrations. ManipTranss evaluation is stochastic, so we fix its evaluation seed, and over three evaluation seeds the standard deviation of its mean ADD-AUC and success rates is at most 0.8 points. On the V2D challenge, the official evaluator runs one rollout per episode from the first frame. It is not deterministic, so we report the mean of four runs. Compute. DexDuet trains each policy for 4,35011,500 PPO updates, which are 1.674.42 transitions on the DexMachina and SPIDER suites and 0.581.51 on the ManipTrans suite, and the ablation rows (b)(g) stop after at most 13,000 updates (4.99 transitions). B.5. Tracking Metrics ADD-AUC. We use DexMachinas released code unchanged. For each part, it samples 500 mesh vertices with fixed seed. For each rollout and frame, it computes the mean distance between these vertices at the reached and at the demonstrated pose. The accuracy at threshold is the share of (rollout, frame) pairs with an error below it, for thresholds of 1, 2, . . . , 9 cm. The AUC is the trapezoidal area under this accuracy curve, and the reported score is the mean of the two parts AUCs. Following the released evaluator, the state after step is compared with frame t1 of the demonstration. On the SPIDER suite, we apply the same definition to the saved object states of every method. We sample 500 vertices per part with seed 42, use thresholds of 1, 2, . . . , 9 cm and average the AUCs of the two parts. The moving part is placed by the joint angle. As in SPIDERs comparison with DexMachina, the state after each step is compared with the frame of the demonstration that this step tracks. On SPIDERs released trajectories, this gives scores close to those SPIDER reports (Sec. D). On the ManipTrans suite, ADD-AUC is computed over each 200-frame window. Success rates and MPPE. For each rollout, this code averages the position error and the geodesic rotation error of each object part over all frames, with the frame alignment of ADD-AUC. MPPE places six points 5 cm from the origin of each part along its axes and averages their distance over frames, parts and rollouts.
